topicTitle: Specialized Data Collections (Map, Set, WeakMap, WeakSet)

lessons.title: Keyed Collections: Map vs Object
lessons.description: Map stores key-value pairs with any type as key — more flexible than plain objects.

sections.heading: Why Map over Object?
paragraphs: Objects only accept string/symbol keys. Maps accept any value — objects, functions, primitives — as keys. They also maintain insertion order and have a size property.
list: Map keys can be any type; Object keys are strings/symbols only
Map has a .size property; objects need Object.keys().length
Maps are optimized for frequent additions/deletions
Maps don't have prototype pollution risks

codeExamples.heading: Map basics
explanation: Maps accept any value as a key — not just strings.
.set() adds entries, .get() retrieves them, .has() checks existence.
.size gives the count directly — no extra calculation needed.
Maps are iterable — use for...of, forEach, or spread.

practice.task: Create a Map that stores user objects as keys and their permissions as values. Iterate over all entries.

keyTakeaways: Maps accept any value as a key — objects, functions, primitives.
Maps are optimized for frequent additions and deletions.
Maps maintain insertion order and have a .size property.
lessons.challenge: Build a caching function that uses a Map to store results keyed by the input arguments.

lessons.title: Managing Unique Sets with Set
lessons.description: Set stores unique values — perfect for deduplication, membership checks and set operations.

sections.heading: Set basics
list: Sets are iterable — use for...of, spread, forEach

codeExamples.heading: Set for deduplication and operations
explanation: Spread a Set into an array to deduplicate: [...new Set(arr)].
Filter for intersection: keep values both sets have.
Spread both sets for union: combine all values.
Sets make these operations clean and readable.

practice.task: Given two arrays, find common elements using Set. Then find elements unique to each array.

keyTakeaways: Sets store only unique values — duplicates are automatically removed.
Sets are perfect for deduplication, membership checks and set operations.
lessons.challenge: Implement symmetric difference (elements in either set but not both) using Set operations.

lessons.title: Garbage Collection Integration: WeakMap & WeakSet
lessons.description: WeakMap and WeakSet allow garbage collection of their entries when there are no other references.

sections.heading: WeakMap and WeakSet
list: WeakMap — keys must be objects; entries are weakly held
WeakSet — values must be objects; entries are weakly held
When no other references to a key/value exist, it's garbage collected
Not iterable — you can't loop over them (by design)

codeExamples.heading: WeakMap for private data
explanation: WeakMap stores private data keyed by the object instance.
When the object is garbage collected, the WeakMap entry is automatically removed.
This prevents memory leaks — no cleanup code needed.
WeakMap is not iterable — it's designed for private/hidden data.

practice.task: Use a WeakMap to store a 'created' timestamp for objects. When the object is garbage collected, the entry should be cleaned up automatically.

keyTakeaways: WeakMap and WeakSet hold weak references — entries are garbage collected when unreferenced.
Keys (WeakMap) and values (WeakSet) must be objects.
They're not iterable — designed for private data and caching.
Perfect for associating metadata with objects without preventing garbage collection.
lessons.challenge: Build a memoization cache using WeakMap that automatically cleans up when the input object is garbage collected.
